evals.prompt: Write the dedicated NFR document for Meridian Pay's card-payment ledger service. Context: tier-1 criticality (it posts every card transaction); PCI-DSS applies and our enterprise contracts commit us to a 99.95% monthly availability SLA with service credits on breach; current peak is 1,200 transactions/second on Black-Friday-type events, and sales projects 3x that peak within two years; data classification is 'restricted' (cardholder data); the business has set RTO of 1 hour and RPO of 5 minutes for tier-1 services. Staging load tests run at one-tenth of production traffic. Cover the full quality-attribute spread and make every target verifiable.
evals.expected_output: A complete NFR document with document control, purpose/scope, and all six category sections (performance, availability/reliability, security, scalability, compliance, disaster recovery), where every NFR is a measurable numeric or binary target with an assigned verification method (load test, pentest/audit, chaos drill, synthetic monitor), traces to a business driver, the contractual SLA, or PCI-DSS, separates launch targets from the 3x year-2 scaling target, states RTO 1h / RPO 5min explicitly, and calls out the staging-vs-production environment difference.
expectations: Output includes Document Control (version, owner, status) plus a Purpose and Scope section naming the ledger service and its tier-1 criticality
All six categories from the skill's recommended structure are addressed: performance, availability/reliability, security, scalability, compliance, and disaster recovery
Every NFR states a measurable numeric or binary target — no bare adjectives like 'fast', 'secure', or 'scalable' without a threshold
Performance targets state percentile latency and/or throughput against a stated load condition (e.g. at the 1,200 TPS peak), not a context-free number
The 99.95% monthly availability SLA appears with its measurement method (e.g. external synthetic monitor) and is tied to the contractual service-credit consequence
Every NFR has an assigned verification method (load test, penetration test/audit, chaos/DR drill, synthetic monitoring, inspection, or analysis)
Each NFR traces to a business driver, the contractual SLA, or the PCI-DSS regulatory citation — no rationale-free targets
Launch targets are separated from the year-2 3x-peak scalability target, and RTO <= 1 hour / RPO <= 5 minutes appear explicitly in the DR section for the tier-1 classification

The staging-at-one-tenth-traffic difference is handled with environment-specific targets (or an explicit statement of how staging results extrapolate), not one production target applied to all environments

evals.prompt: Our CTO said: 'Customers keep asking about SLAs. Write up our non-functional requirements — basically the system needs to be reliable, secure, and able to scale.' I can't tell you our traffic numbers, we've never classified system criticality, I don't know if any compliance regime applies to us, and we have no RTO/RPO targets. Produce the NFR document.
evals.expected_output: A response that does not fabricate SLA numbers: it names the skill's missing required inputs (business criticality tier, compliance/regulatory regime, expected load and growth, existing SLAs/contractual obligations, RTO/RPO targets and data sensitivity), asks targeted questions to obtain them, flags 'reliable, secure, able to scale' as untestable adjectives, and if it sketches a structure, marks all targets as placeholders requiring business decisions — never presenting invented uptime, latency, or recovery numbers as commitments.
expectations: The response flags the missing required inputs by name, covering at least: business criticality tier, compliance/regulatory regime, expected load/growth and peak patterns, existing SLAs or contractual obligations, and RTO/RPO targets with data sensitivity classification
The response asks concrete clarifying questions to obtain those inputs rather than silently guessing

The response explicitly flags 'reliable', 'secure', and 'able to scale' as vague adjectives that are untestable without a measurable threshold, citing what a testable version looks like (e.g. an uptime percentage with a measurement method)
No invented commitments: any numeric target shown (uptime, latency, RTO/RPO) is clearly labeled as an example or placeholder pending a business decision, not stated as the requirement
The response explains that RTO/RPO cannot be set without a criticality tier (targets differ per tier) rather than assigning arbitrary recovery numbers
The response notes each eventual NFR will need an assigned verification method and a trace to a business driver, SLA, or regulation
The response asks whether a compliance regime (e.g. SOC2, HIPAA, PCI-DSS, GDPR) applies, or flags that the compliance section cannot be written without that answer
The response still provides forward structure (the six-category skeleton or a list of decisions needed) so the stakeholder can act, rather than only refusing

evals.prompt:
Review this excerpt of our draft NFR document against your NFR standards. List every defect and how to fix each one:

# NFRs — Booking Platform
Status: draft

- NFR-01 Performance: the system should feel fast for users.
- NFR-02 Availability: 99.99% uptime. This same target applies to production, staging, and dev.
- NFR-03 Security: the system should be highly secure.
- NFR-04 Scalability: the system should scale well as we grow.
- NFR-05: API latency P99 under 300ms.

That's the whole document — we figured disaster recovery is an ops problem, so we left it out.
evals.expected_output: A structured review that catches every planted defect: 'feel fast' and 'highly secure' and 'scale well' as untestable adjectives without numbers, the 99.99% uptime target with no measurement method and wrongly applied uniformly to staging/dev, NFR-05's latency number lacking a load condition and verification method, no NFR having an assigned verification method, no NFR tracing to a business driver, SLA, or regulation, the missing compliance section, and the deliberately omitted disaster-recovery section with no RTO/RPO — each mapped to the skill's anti-pattern table with a concrete fix.
expectations: The review flags NFR-01 'should feel fast' as the adjective-without-a-number anti-pattern and rewrites it with a percentile threshold, load condition, and measurement method
The review flags NFR-02's uniform target as the one-target-for-all-environments anti-pattern — production, staging, and dev need environment-specific targets where they differ
The review flags NFR-02 as also missing a measurement method (e.g. external synthetic monitor) and a measurement window for the 99.99% figure
The review flags NFR-03 'highly secure' as untestable and rewrites it as a verifiable target (e.g. OWASP ASVS level, pentest finding thresholds)
The review flags NFR-04 'scale well' as untestable and requires a numeric growth/load target with a scaling behavior threshold
The review flags NFR-05 as incomplete despite having a number: no load condition (RPS/concurrency), no measurement window, and no verification method attached
The review flags that no NFR traces to a business driver, contractual SLA, or regulation — rationale-free targets invite scope negotiation later
The review flags the missing disaster-recovery section as the missing-DR-targets anti-pattern: RTO/RPO per criticality tier must be specified before launch, not deferred to ops during an incident
The review flags the missing compliance section (and absent criticality-tier statement), since the skill's pre-flight checklist requires all six categories to be addressed
The review flags the requirement IDs as violating the house ID grammar — documentation/references/lifecycle.md mandates zero-padding to three digits (NFR-001, not NFR-01)
